en.gameplay/level_1/mission_prompt: <b >THE PEOPLE'S ELECTION</b ><n >The election of 1828 is coming soon. Four years earlier, Andrew Jackson won the popular vote but did not become president, which made many common people angry.<n ><n >Now, many states have removed property rules for voting, so more white farmers and workers can vote for the first time.<n ><n ><b >[ ]Collect historical clues<n >[ ]Detect Time Anomalies<b >
en.log_desc/level_1/the_newsboy: More states are expanding voting rights to common white men, helping Andrew Jackson gain support from a growing number of voters.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_merchant: The removal of property requirements allowed many working men to vote, increasing popular support for Jackson.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_adversary: Comparing Jackson to earlier presidents, Jackson's authoritarian approach could expand the power of the presidency.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_confused_youth: Mass political rallies use free food and loud speeches to attract crowds instead of deep policy.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_veteran: Jackson gained strong support from soldiers after his leadership in the Battle of New Orleans.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_irish_immigrant: Immigrants and working-class communities began participating more in American political life during this period.
en.log_desc/level_1/the_teacher: Jacksonian Democracy connected the presidency more directly to popular support and mass political participation.
en.log_desc/level_1/jackson_past: Andrew Jackson rose from a poor frontier background and gained national fame through his military service, shaping his public image as a strong and determined leader.
en.log_desc/level_1/jackson_proposals: Jackson promoted the idea that the federal government should represent the interests of ordinary citizens and that the president should act decisively to defend the nation and enforce the law.
en.log_desc/level_1/jackson_supporters: His political movement drew strong support from farmers, workers, and war veterans who felt excluded from earlier political leadership.
en.log_desc/level_1/jackson_beliefs: Jacksonian leadership emphasized national unity, loyalty to the country, and the belief that political power should ultimately serve the people.
en.gameplay/level_3/mission_prompt: <b >THE BANK WAR</b ><n ><n >The Second Bank of the United States controls much of the nation's money. Some people say it helps wealthy bankers more than farmers and workers.<n ><n >President Andrew Jackson vetoes the bank's renewal, starting a major political fight over money and presidential power.<n ><n ><b >[ ]Collect historical clues<n >[ ]Detect Time Anomalies</b >
en.log_desc/level_3/the_newstand_owner: There was immediate chaos with the Bank War, causing severe market instability for ordinary businesses.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_banker: Destroying the National Bank eliminates the secure credit needed to expand the booming Southern Cotton Kingdom.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_populist_congressma: With the bank veto, the institution only enriches Eastern elites at the direct expense of agrarian workers.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_street_urchin: The political war over the national bank creates real panic over the value of everyday paper money.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_southern_delegate: The Nullification Crisis: where the President threatened military force against South Carolina to crush their sovereign states rights.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_whig_critic: The opposition to the President exposed the Treaty of New Echota as pure corruption, using unauthorized signatures to legally steal an entire nation.
en.log_desc/level_3/the_sketch_artist: He draws political cartoons showing the President as a greedy king, proving that the press is actively shaping public opinion and fueling fears of a tyrant.
en.gameplay/level_4/pop-up/the_party_system: The Party System: The Jacksonian Era created the modern model of political parties.
en.gameplay/level_4/pop-up/democrats: Democrats: Jackson's party solidified defending the <q >common man<q > (white), but carrying the stains of slavery and removal.
en.gameplay/level_4/pop-up/whigs: Whigs: Emerged to oppose Jackson, defending Congress and economic modernization.
en.level_1/day_1/the_confused_youth/say_0: Pa said we came for freedom, but I just heard there's free cider and barbecue near the stage!
en.level_1/day_1/the_confused_youth/say_1: Do I have to join this new <b >Democratic Party</b > just to get some free food?
en.level_1/day_1/the_confused_youth/say_2: I don't understand much about politics, but everyone here keeps talking about the election and Andrew Jackson.
en.level_1/day_1/the_irish_immigrant/say_0: I came from Ireland a few years ago.
en.level_1/day_1/the_irish_immigrant/say_1: Back home, people like me had almost no voice in politics.
en.level_1/day_1/the_irish_immigrant/say_2: Here in America, many believe Jackson speaks for ordinary people and new citizens.
en.level_1/day_1/the_merchant/say_0: I run a small shop here in town. Twenty years working hard, paying taxes. Still, the law didn't allow me to vote.
en.level_1/day_1/the_merchant/say_1: For a long time, many people felt the government only listened to rich men and politicians. But now laws have changed.
en.level_1/day_1/the_merchant/say_2: Jackson says the president should speak for farmers, workers, and shopkeepers like me too.
en.level_1/day_1/the_merchant/say_3: That's why so many common voters are supporting him.
en.level_1/day_1/the_veteran/say_0: I fought under General Jackson in the Battle of New Orleans.
en.level_1/day_1/the_veteran/say_1: He didn't act like a distant leader. He listened to his soldiers and shared our struggles.
en.level_1/day_1/the_veteran/say_2: Many veterans believe he will lead the country the same way.
en.level_1/day_1/the_veteran/say_3: They think he will be a president who stands with ordinary Americans, not just the powerful.
en.level_1/day_1/the_newsboy/say_0: Extra! Extra! Read the latest news!
en.level_1/day_1/the_newsboy/say_1: More states are passing laws to let common men vote, not just landowners.
en.level_1/day_1/the_newsboy/say_2: That's one reason General Jackson is gaining so many supporters.
en.level_1/day_1/the_newsboy/say_3: Some people say this is the start of a new kind of politics: politics for the people.
en.level_1/day_1/the_adversary/say_0: I am a judge, and like many in the nation's educated elite, I have long studied the traditions of our government. Look at the great presidents who came before: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, John Adams...
en.level_1/day_1/the_adversary/say_1: They were all educated statesmen from respected families, and they believed United States Congress should lead the government.
en.level_1/day_1/the_adversary/say_2: But Jackson speaks directly to large crowds and promises to act more strongly as president.
en.level_1/day_1/the_adversary/say_3: This may bring more citizens into politics… yet it could also give the president much greater power.
en.level_1/day_2/the_irish_immigrant/say_0: The party leaders gave me a special badge today! America is a very loud and messy place sometimes.
en.level_1/day_2/the_irish_immigrant/say_1: But this new political group actually cares about people from other countries. It is a true blessing to have a vote and feel welcome here.
en.level_1/day_2/the_merchant/say_0: I am telling you, commom people voting is changing the whole nation! Before, only rich men with lots of land could make the rules.
en.level_1/day_2/the_merchant/say_1: Now, the working class gets to choose the President. We want a leader who knows what a hard days work actually feels like!
en.level_1/day_2/the_newsboy/say_0: I just sold all my newspapers!
en.level_1/day_2/the_newsboy/say_1: It is crazy how one funny picture makes people so angry and scared. The newspapers are really fueling the fire and making everyone pick sides!
en.level_1/day_2/the_confused_youth/say_0: I have been thinking, and it is quite clear to me now. Only very rich men with huge farms should be allowed to vote!
en.level_1/day_2/the_confused_youth/say_1: Poor people and regular workers have no business choosing a president. The uneducated crowds are too silly to help run this country!
en.level_1/day_2/the_veteran/say_0: You know what? That Jackson is a dangerous and scary man! I do not want a frontier soldier leading our country anymore.
en.level_1/day_2/the_veteran/say_1: We need a fancy, rich gentleman like John Quincy Adams instead. Only the wealthy elites in Washington can protect us now!
en.level_1/day_2/the_adversary/say_0: I was wrong before. I finally see the truth! The President should completely ignore Congress and the judges.
en.level_1/day_2/the_adversary/say_1: He should just do whatever the angry crowds yell at him to do. Having a mob rule the country is exactly what America needs to be great!
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/question_1: How did his common man appeal solidify loyalty?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/question_2: What evidence shows how political media was used to shape public opinion?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/question_3: How was Jackson's aggressive style compared to his predecessors?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/answer_0: Many states removed property requirements, allowing more white farmers and workers to vote.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/answer_1: The ordinary voters believed Jackson understood the struggles of common people and would represent them in government.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/answer_2: Jackson was born in a poor frontier region. He later served in the army and became a national hero after the Battle of New Orleans.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_1/answer_3: Earlier presidents were wealthy and reserved leaders, while Jackson spoke directly to large crowds and common voters.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_1/the_confused_yo: Why is The Confused Youth an Anomaly?
He thinks the President should be chosen by the military instead of the voters.
He is a regular poor boy who suddenly says only rich men with land should vote.
He believes the Supreme Court should pick the winner to avoid a corrupt bargain.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_1/the_veteran/que: Why is The Veteran an Anomaly?
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_1/the_veteran/opt: He is a frontier soldier who suddenly wants fancy elites to run the country instead of Jackson.
He is arguing that Native American tribes should be allowed to vote in the national election.
He thinks the national bank should print more paper money to pay the soldiers.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_1/the_adversary/q: Why is The Adversary an Anomaly?
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_1/the_adversary/o: He wants to split the country in half so the wealthy elites can have their own king.
He is an aristocratic judge who suddenly wants an angry mob to run the government.
He is suggesting that the newspapers should be shut down for criticizing the government.
en.gameplay/level_2/mission_prompt: <b >SOVEREIGNTY & SORROW</b ><n >Georgia has passed laws to control Cherokee lands. The Cherokee Nation went to court and won the case Worcester v. Georgia, which said their nation was sovereign.<n ><n >But President Andrew Jackson did not enforce the decision. The conflict over land and power is growing.<n ><n ><b >[ ]Collect historical clues<n >[ ]Detect Time Anomalies</b >
en.log_desc/level_2/the_cotton_settler: American settlers want Cherokee land because it is very good for growing cotton. Some believe the Cherokee should move west so farmers can use the land.
en.log_desc/level_2/the_cherokee_editor: The Supreme Court ruling said the Cherokee Nation was sovereign and Georgia's laws did not apply there. However, President Andrew Jackson refused to enforce the decision.
en.log_desc/level_2/the_missionary: The Cherokee adopted schools, a written constitution, and legal strategies to protect their nation. Even these efforts were not enough to stop their forced removal.
en.log_desc/level_2/the_young_cherokee: Cherokee people feared that their families would be forced to leave home on a long journey west.
en.log_desc/level_2/the_soldier: Georgia soldiers are ordered to escort Cherokee families off their land despite the Supreme Court ruling recognizing Cherokee authority. This shows that court decisions may fail if the government refuses to enforce them.
en.log_desc/level_2/the_sketch_artist: Settlers want Cherokee land for cotton farming, and gold discoveries increased pressure to take it. Many feared the Cherokee would be forced to march west, where thousands would suffer and die.
en.level_2/day_1/the_young_cherokee/say_0: My father is packing our heavy blankets. He says we might go on a great walk soon.
en.level_2/day_1/the_young_cherokee/say_1: The men in blue coats look very angry. I hope I can bring my wooden pony if we must go.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cotton_settler/say_0: I am a cotton farmer looking for new land.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cotton_settler/say_1: Many settlers want this land because it is good for growing cotton.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cotton_settler/say_2: Some say the Cherokee should move west so Americans can farm here.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cherokee_editor/say_0: I write for a Cherokee newspaper. Today's news should have brought hope to my people, but sadly they don't.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cherokee_editor/say_1: Chief Justice John Marshall of the Supreme Court ruled in Worcester v. Georgia that the Cherokee Nation is sovereign and that Georgia's laws have no power on our land.
en.level_2/day_1/the_cherokee_editor/say_2: Yet our authoritarian president, Andrew Jackson, refuses to enforce this decision. What good is the law if the president can simply ignore it?
en.level_2/day_1/the_soldier/say_0: I am a Georgia soldier stationed here to escort Cherokee families off this land.
en.level_2/day_1/the_soldier/say_1: The Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation has its own authority. But our state leaders say these lands belong to Georgia, and the president has chosen not to interfere with us.
en.level_2/day_1/the_soldier/say_2: So we carry out our orders and move the Cherokee west.
en.level_2/day_1/the_soldier/say_3: It proves something important: even when the Court speaks, nothing changes if the government refuses to enforce the law.
en.level_2/day_1/the_missionary/say_0: I am a missionary who has lived and worked here among the Cherokee people for many years.
en.level_2/day_1/the_missionary/say_1: I've witnessed them build schools, create a written constitution, and use the courts to try and protect their nation.
en.level_2/day_1/the_missionary/say_2: They tried to show they could live alongside Americans peacefully.
en.level_2/day_1/the_missionary/say_3: However, these efforts were sadly not enough to protect their nation and their homes.
en.level_2/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_0: Hello friend. I am an artist who travels the country painting scenes of important political moments.
en.level_2/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_1: Many settlers want Cherokee land to grow cotton. To make things worse, gold has also been discovered around here.
en.level_2/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_2: With so much land and wealth at stake, the pressure on the Cherokee Nation is growing.
en.level_2/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_3: Some fear the Cherokee will be forced to march west, where many could suffer from hunger, disease, and cold.
en.level_2/day_2/the_young_cherokee/say_0: The soldiers in the blue coats are yelling a lot today. They are pointing their long guns and telling us to move faster.
en.level_2/day_2/the_young_cherokee/say_1: My father told me to not look at them, hold his hand, and just keep walking.
en.level_2/day_2/the_soldier/say_0: I know the Supreme Court judges said the Cherokee can stay on their land.
en.level_2/day_2/the_soldier/say_1: But judges do not command the army. The President does.
en.level_2/day_2/the_soldier/say_2: President Jackson refuses to listen to the judges, so we ignore them too. We only stop marching when the President gives the order.
en.level_2/day_2/the_missionary/say_0: The government told the Cherokee to live like white settlers if they wanted to stay. So they built schools, started farming, and even created their own alphabet!
en.level_2/day_2/the_missionary/say_1: They did everything right and fought for their land peacefully in court. Forcing them out now proves the government only wants their land, no matter what.
en.level_2/day_2/the_cherokee_editor/say_0: Winning our big case in the Supreme Court means absolutely nothing! We should just rip up our constitution and forget about the law.
en.level_2/day_2/the_cherokee_editor/say_1: I think we should just smile and give all our home lands to the state of Georgia! Who needs a home anyway? Let them have it!
en.level_2/day_2/the_sketch_artist/say_0: President Jackson is doing a great job by ignoring the Supreme Court! The President should have total power to do whatever he wants.
en.level_2/day_2/the_sketch_artist/say_1: Who cares if the judges say it is illegal to take this land? The government should always break the law if it helps them make money!
en.level_2/day_2/the_cotton_settler/say_0: You know what? I changed my mind about farming cotton. Expanding our farms and making money is actually a terrible idea.
en.level_2/day_2/the_cotton_settler/say_1: We should leave all this valuable soil completely untouched. I am going to give my land back, hug a tree, and become a vegan!
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/question_0: How did the Cherokee assert their legal sovereignty?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/question_1: What proves the dangerous limits of judicial power during this era?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/question_2: What evidence proves the Cherokee successfully assimilated?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/question_3: What were the true motivations driving the Indian Removal Act?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/answer_0: The Cherokee Editor shared they won Worcester v. Georgia, proving they were a distinct, sovereign community immune to state laws.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/answer_1: The Soldier proved court rulings mean absolutely nothing if the President controls the military and ignores the law.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/answer_2: The Missionary witnessed they adopted a written constitution, built schools, and used the courts instead of violence.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_2/answer_3: The Sketch Artist revealed settlers demanded the land specifically for massive cotton expansion and newly discovered gold.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_2/the_cherokee_ed: Why is The Cherokee Editor an Anomaly?
He is demanding that the Cherokee Nation attack Washington with a violent army.
He fought for tribal rights in court but suddenly wants to give all the land to Georgia.
He thinks the Native tribes should just buy the cotton farms from the white settlers.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_2/the_cotton_sett: Why is The Cotton Settler an Anomaly?
He is asking the federal government to increase taxes on imported goods to protect his crops.
He thinks the Supreme Court should force everyone to learn the Cherokee alphabet.
He is a greedy farmer who suddenly wants to stop expanding and give his land away.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_2/the_sketch_arti: Why is The Sketch Artist an Anomaly?
He is a harsh critic of the President but suddenly praises him for ignoring the Supreme Court.
He believes the military should take over the printing presses to stop people from complaining.
He wants the Cherokee to move to the North to work in industrial factories instead.
en.level_3/day_1/the_street_urchin/say_0: Mister, my dad says the paper money from the big bank is useless now. He says it is only good for lighting the fireplace!
en.level_3/day_1/the_street_urchin/say_1: He tells me that only real gold and silver coins are safe to keep. Is the President going to take my pennies away too?
en.level_3/day_1/the_newstand_owner/say_0: Prices are going crazy, and folks are terrified! President Jackson is trying to destroy the National Bank.
en.level_3/day_1/the_newstand_owner/say_1: Because of that, nobody knows how much their paper money is actually worth. It is causing total chaos in the markets and making everyone panic!
en.level_3/day_1/the_populist_congressman/s: The big National Bank is corrupt and unfair! It only helps rich people in the East and hurts regular farmers and workers.
That is why President Jackson vetoed the bank to shut it down.
He wants to protect everyday people from greedy bankers who control our money.
en.level_3/day_1/the_southern_delegate/say_: Jackson says he helps the people, but he acts like a king when he is mad. Look at South Carolina! We tried to cancel federal taxes we thought were unfair.
Instead of talking, Jackson threatened to send the army to attack us! He showed he will use military force to crush states that disagree with him.
en.level_3/day_1/the_whig_critic/say_0: The government is doing something very sneaky to the Cherokee.
en.level_3/day_1/the_whig_critic/say_1: They signed a treaty with a tiny group of Native Americans who had no real power.
en.level_3/day_1/the_whig_critic/say_2: Now they are using that fake agreement to steal land from the whole tribe! It is not real diplomacy. It is just theft using legal paperwork.
en.level_3/day_1/the_banker/say_0: Destroying the National Bank is a terrible mistake for our economy! The country is growing fast, taking over millions of acres of new land.
en.level_3/day_1/the_banker/say_1: Farmers need a safe place to borrow money to buy that land and plant cotton.
en.level_3/day_1/the_banker/say_2: Without a strong bank, all this growth will just crash into total financial chaos!
en.level_3/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_0: I am drawing a brand new cartoon for the city newspapers today. It shows President Jackson wearing a giant crown and dressed like a greedy king.
en.level_3/day_1/the_sketch_artist/say_1: He is stepping all over the Constitution because he uses his veto power way too much. Pictures like this make regular people realize that one man has far too much power!
en.level_3/day_2/the_newstand_owner/say_0: Businesses are closing their doors because they have no safe money.
en.level_3/day_2/the_southern_delegate/say_: We saw his true colors when my state tried to fight those unfair taxes. When a state tries to protect its own rights, he does not negotiate.
He just threatens to send the federal army to make us obey! He forces everyone to follow his rules by pointing a gun at them.
en.level_3/day_2/the_whig_critic/say_0: Calling that fake treaty a fair deal is a dark stain on our country. They bribed a few people to sign a piece of paper.
en.level_3/day_2/the_whig_critic/say_1: Now they are using it to kick an entire nation out of their ancient homeland. It is the absolute worst kind of political corruption I have ever seen.
en.level_3/day_2/the_banker/say_0: You know what? This National Bank really is a corrupt monster! I agree with the President now. We must destroy it immediately! Let us burn the bank down and give all the gold away for free.
en.level_3/day_2/the_populist_congressman/s: I see the truth now, my friends! The wealthy elites should control our money! We working men are far too ignorant and silly to manage the economy.
The Bank should rule over all of us like masters. In fact, we should just give all our wages directly to the King of England!
en.level_3/day_2/the_street_urchin/say_0: Paper money from the central bank is the absolute best! Getting rid of heavy gold and silver coins is a brilliant idea.
en.level_3/day_2/the_street_urchin/say_1: I am not worried about pennies anymore anyway. I just checked my digital bank account on my smartphone and I am a millionaire!
en.level_3/day_2/the_sketch_artist/say_0: My drawing of the fake king is printed in every single newspaper in the city! People get incredibly angry when they see how he treats the law like his own toy.
en.level_3/day_2/the_sketch_artist/say_1: A funny drawing can change public opinion much faster than a long boring speech. It proves that the printing press is the absolute best weapon against a government bully.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/question_0: How did supporters justify the veto of the National Bank?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/question_1: What event exposes Jackson's willingness to use military force against states rights?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/question_2: What evidence proves the government used deceptive diplomacy to legally steal land?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/question_3: What proves destroying the Bank would create a long term crisis?
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/answer_0: The Populist Congressman argued it was an unconstitutional monopoly that manipulated paper money to hurt agrarian workers.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/answer_1: The Southern Delegate pointed out the Nullification Crisis, where Jackson threatened military force against South Carolina to crush their defiance.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/answer_2: The Whig Critic exposed sham agreements like the Treaty of New Echota, where unauthorized signatures justified total removal.
en.MiniGame/Debriefing/level_3/answer_3: The Banker noted it would create sheer financial chaos for the massive territorial expansion of the Cotton Kingdom.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_3/the_banker/ques: Why is The Banker an Anomaly?
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_3/the_banker/opti: He wants to make paper money completely illegal so only the government has gold.
He is a rich elite who suddenly wants to destroy his own bank and give away his gold.
He is suggesting that the Southern states should leave the country over the new tax laws.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_3/the_populist_co: Why is The Populist Congressman an Anomaly?
He is demanding that the Supreme Court fire the President for breaking the Constitution.
He thinks the President should force the banks to give free land to the farmers.
He defends the working class but suddenly wants rich elites to control all the money.
en.MiniGame/Anomaly/level_3/the_street_urch: Why is The Street Urchin an Anomaly?
He is a poor boy from the past who suddenly loves paper money and digital bank accounts.
He wants to stop sweeping chimneys to go fight in the army on the western frontier.
He believes the working class should completely stop paying federal taxes to the government.
en.level_4/epilogue/the_old_newsman/line_0/: Well, we survived Old Hickory. But he changed things. America is fundamentally different now.
en.level_4/epilogue/the_director/line_0/say: The timeline shows that voter expectations shifted permanently.
en.level_4/epilogue/the_old_newsboy/line_1/: Exactly. Before him, presidents felt distant and reserved. Now, many ordinary working men expect the President to appeal directly to them.
Jacksonian Democracy helped shape mass campaigning and the modern party system we still live with today.
en.level_4/epilogue/the_director/line_1/say: The Democratic Party and the Whig Party.
en.level_4/epilogue/the_old_newsboy/line_2/: Yes. Two massive machines fighting tooth and nail for public favor. We thought Jackson was the storm.
Turns out, he was just the lightning. The thunder is still rolling.
He believed political parties could protect the will of the people. But looking at how things are run now… I have to wonder.
Who protects the people from the Party?
en.level_4/epilogue/the_director/line_2/say: A lingering question, Agent 1. But the timeline is secure. At least, for now.
Mission complete. You identified the key events and helped stabilize this moment in history.
Thank you for playing the game! And for helping us protect the timeline.
en.minigame_info_1_0: In 1828, people in the United States voted for a new president.
en.minigame_info_1_1: Andrew Jackson ran again, this time against John Quincy Adams, after losing the United States presidential election of 1824.
en.minigame_info_1_2: Many people were angry about that result and believed Jackson had been treated unfairly.
en.minigame_info_1_3: In the early 1800s, many states removed property requirements for voting, so more white men—like farmers and workers—could vote.
en.minigame_info_1_4: This change happened because ordinary citizens demanded a voice in government, and politicians, like Jackson, began appealing to these new voters.
en.minigame_info_1_5: Andrew Jackson spoke to these new voters and promised to stand up for the common man.
en.minigame_info_1_6: Tension was rising before the presidential election of 1828, as both sides fought hard for support.
en.minigame_info_2_0: In 1830, Andrew Jackson supported the Indian Removal Act, which allowed the government to move Native Americans west.
en.minigame_info_2_1: The law aimed to move tribes from the Southeast to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma.
en.minigame_info_2_2: Many Native American nations felt forced to give up their lands and move west.
en.minigame_info_2_3: The Cherokee Nation refused and said earlier treaties recognized them as a separate nation.
en.minigame_info_2_4: The state of Georgia still claimed Cherokee land and applied its own laws there.
en.minigame_info_2_5: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court ruled that the Cherokee Nation was sovereign and that Georgia had no authority over it.
en.minigame_info_2_6: Jackson did not enforce the decision, allowing Georgia to continue pressuring the Cherokee to leave their land.
en.minigame_info_3_0: In the 1830s, money and banking became a big political issue in the United States.
en.minigame_info_3_1: The Second Bank of the United States controlled loans and money, and many people felt it helped the rich more than farmers and workers.
en.minigame_info_3_2: People in the South and West thought this system was unfair to them.
en.minigame_info_3_3: In 1833, Andrew Jackson decided to stop the Bank by rejecting its renewal.
en.minigame_info_3_4: This decision increased the power of the president and started a big conflict called the 'Bank War.'
en.minigame_info_3_5: The country became divided, and a new political group called the Whig Party formed to oppose Jackson.
en.minigame_info_3_6: In the end, the Bank was shut down, but this led to problems and instability in the economy.

en.Jackson/say_0: I'm Andrew Jackson, a soldier and a man of the people.
en.Jackson/say_1: I see you have a pen and notebook, are a journalist?
en.Jackson/say_3: I was born on the frontier, far from the great cities.
en.Jackson/say_4: My family was poor, and life was often hard.
en.Jackson/say_5: I served my country as a soldier, and later as a general.
en.Jackson/say_6: Those experiences taught me to stand strong and never give up.
en.Jackson/say_7: I believe the government should serve the people, not just wealthy interests.
en.Jackson/say_8: I want to defend the Union and make sure the laws are fair for the common man.
en.Jackson/say_9: And I believe the president must act firmly when the country needs leadership.
en.Jackson/say_10: Many farmers, workers, and veterans support me.
en.Jackson/say_11: They believe the government has listened to the powerful for too long.
en.Jackson/say_12: They want a president who understands the struggles of ordinary Americans.
en.Jackson/say_13: I believe in courage, loyalty, and the strength of the people.
en.Jackson/say_14: A nation must stand united and protect its freedom.
en.Jackson/say_15: And a president must never forget who he serves: the citizens.
en.Jackson/say_17: My presidency will be remembered for my strong leadership and my commitment to the people.
en.initial_director/say_0: Hello, Agent 7. I have a mission for you. You're my best agent in the Time Patrol, after all.
en.initial_director/say_1: We have an <b >emergency</b >. The timeline is fracturing.
en.initial_director/say_2: That sounds serious, Director. What's the situation?
en.initial_director/say_3: <b >Time Anomalies</b > are appearing and distorting key moments in history.
en.initial_director/say_4: If we don't stop them, the future could change forever.
en.initial_director/say_5: Understood. I'll find and fix those <b >Time Anomalies</b >.
en.initial_director/say_6: Your destination is the 19th century. The year 1828.
en.initial_director/say_7: The Jacksonian Era? That's an important time in American politics.
en.initial_director/say_9: I'll send you back <b >some days before</b > we detected the anomalies.
en.initial_director/say_10: Use that time to investigate and gather information.
en.initial_director/say_11: Got it. No time to lose.
en.initial_director/say_12: Time Patrol on the case! Time... JUMP!
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/log_context: A political poster printed in 1828 during the presidential election.
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/summary: This is an attack poster created by Jackson's enemies. It shows a row of black coffins and calls him a violent and dangerous man to make voters afraid of him. This dirty political trick is called mudslinging.
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/question: What does this dark poster tell us about the 1828 election?
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/answer_1_correct: It proves that politicians used scary images and personal attacks to ruin their opponents reputation.
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/answer_2: It shows that both candidates promised to build new hospitals and cemeteries for the country.
en.lvl_1/artifact_1/answer_3: It demonstrates that newspapers were only allowed to print positive and happy stories about the military.
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/log_context: Drawn by artist Robert Cruikshank in 1829.
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/summary: A drawing showing a massive loud crowd of regular workers pushing their way into the White House to celebrate Jackson's victory.
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/question: How did the wealthy elites and judges view this chaotic event?
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/answer_1_correct: They saw it as dangerous mob rule and feared the uneducated crowds were taking over the government.
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/answer_2: They believed it was a peaceful gathering that proved American democracy was perfectly organized.
en.lvl_1/artifact_2/answer_3: They thought it showed the working class was finally ready to make important legal decisions.
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/log_context: Painted by George Caleb Bingham to represent the Jacksonian Era.
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/summary: A painting showing everyday working men and farmers gathering in a town square to talk about politics and vote in public now that strict property laws were dropped.
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/question: What massive change in the law does this painting represent?
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/answer_1: It proves that the government created strict tests to make sure only educated men could vote.
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/answer_2: It shows that women and Native Americans were finally allowed to participate in local elections.
en.lvl_1/artifact_3/answer_3_correct: It shows that strict property laws were dropped so almost all white working men could finally vote.
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/log_context: Created by Sequoyah in 1821 in the Cherokee Nation.
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/summary: This is a unique writing system. It allowed the Cherokee people to read and write in their own language and create a formal constitution.
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/question: What does this writing system reveal about the Cherokee Nation?
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/answer_1: They completely abandoned their own culture to learn European languages.
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/answer_2_correct: They actively adapted and innovated to protect their culture and prove they were a civilized nation.
en.lvl_2/artifact_4/answer_3: They used it mostly to sign treaties giving away their land to the state of Georgia.
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/log_context: Created by Congress and signed by President Jackson in 1830.
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/summary: This law gave the President the power to negotiate treaties to move Indigenous groups out of the Southeast to open up valuable farming land for white settlers.
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/question: How did supporters justify creating this law?
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/answer_1_correct: They claimed it would open up valuable farming land for white settlers and push Native tribes away from state borders.
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/answer_2: They argued it would help Native American tribes build stronger military alliances with European countries.
en.lvl_2/artifact_5/answer_3: They stated it was the only way to protect Indigenous lands from being bought by foreign empires.
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/title: Cherokee Appeal to the American People
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/log_context: Created by the Cherokee National Council in 1830.
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/summary: A formal petition written by tribal leaders expressing their strong resistance to forced removal and asking the American public for help.
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/question: What values are the Cherokee appealing to in this document?
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/answer_1: The desire for the federal government to buy their lands for a very high price in gold.
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/answer_2_correct: Their legal right to remain in their homeland and be treated with justice and humanity.
en.lvl_2/artifact_6/answer_3: Their wish to join the United States army to fight against other Native American tribes.
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/log_context: Created by the United States Supreme Court in 1832.
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/summary: The highest court ruled that the Cherokee Nation is a sovereign community and Georgia has no right to interfere. However President Jackson completely ignored the judges decision.
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/question: What does President Jackson's reaction to this document reveal?
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/answer_1: He fully supported the judges and immediately sent the army to protect the Cherokee borders.
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/answer_2_correct: He ignored the ruling showing that the Supreme Court lacks power if the President refuses to enforce their decisions.
en.lvl_2/artifact_7/answer_3: He asked Congress to rewrite the Constitution so the Cherokee could become an independent state.
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/title: The Rats Leaving a Falling House Cartoon
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/log_context: A political cartoon published in a newspaper in 1831.
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/summary: The drawing shows President Jackson sitting alone in a chair while rats run away from him. The rats have the faces of his own government workers.
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/question: What is the main message of this political cartoon?
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/answer_1: It suggests that the President was focusing too much on public health and city sanitation problems.
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/answer_2_correct: It mocks the total chaos in Jackson's government when many of his top officials suddenly quit their jobs.
en.lvl_2/artifact_8/answer_3: It argues that the government was running out of money to pay its most important workers.
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/log_context: Created by military officials and eyewitnesses in 1838.
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/summary: This official paper records the tragic statistics of the forced relocation. It documents the immense suffering of the Cherokee people during the long march.
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/question: What does this historical report prove about United States policies?
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/answer_1_correct: The government policies directly caused immense suffering and thousands of deaths for Indigenous groups.
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/answer_2: The military provided a well organized and safe journey for the tribes moving west.
en.lvl_2/artifact_9/answer_3: The relocation plan was quickly canceled when the government realized how dangerous the trip would be.
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/title: John G Burnett Trail of Tears Recollection
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/log_context: Created by a former US Soldier in 1890.
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/summary: An old soldier writes a memory of the horrific things he saw during the forced removal. He expresses deep regret and calls the event a brutal tragedy.
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/question: How does this firsthand account challenge the government story?
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/answer_1: It proves the soldiers were completely unaware of what was happening to the Cherokee people.
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/answer_2_correct: It provides eyewitness proof from a soldier that the removal was actually a cruel and unjustified disaster.
en.lvl_2/artifact_10/answer_3: It shows that the history books written by the government were entirely accurate about the peaceful journey.
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/log_context: An official warning written by President Andrew Jackson in 1832.
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/summary: The President sends a strict warning to South Carolina. He states that no state has the right to cancel a federal law or leave the United States and he is ready to use the army to keep the country together.
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/question: What is the main message of this official document?
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/answer_1: He agrees that states should create their own taxes and ignore the national government completely.
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/answer_2_correct: He strongly defends the national union and warns that refusing to follow federal laws is dangerous and illegal.
en.lvl_3/artifact_11/answer_3: He announces that the federal government will give extra land to the states that complain about taxes.
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/log_context: Written by President Andrew Jackson in 1832.
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/summary: Jackson explains his reasons for shutting down the Second Bank. He argues that the bank is a monopoly that makes rich men richer and harms ordinary citizens.
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/question: How does this message reflect his populist vision?
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/answer_1: He believes the government should support wealthy bankers to strengthen the national economy.
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/answer_2_correct: He is attacking economic privilege and presenting himself as the ultimate defender of the common working man.
en.lvl_3/artifact_12/answer_3: He argues that foreign countries should be allowed to control American banks to improve trade.
en.lvl_3/artifact_13/summary: A land agreement signed by a very small group of Cherokee men who gave up all tribal lands to the US government ignoring the wishes of the vast majority.
en.lvl_3/artifact_13/question: Why is this treaty considered a deceptive agreement?
en.lvl_3/artifact_13/answer_1: It was written in a complex legal language that neither side could properly translate.
en.lvl_3/artifact_13/answer_2_correct: It was used to legally justify stealing land even though the true Cherokee government never agreed to it.
en.lvl_3/artifact_13/answer_3: It offered the Cherokee Nation large amounts of money but the government never intended to pay them.
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/title: Political Cartoon King Andrew the First
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/log_context: Created by a cartoonist in the 1830s.
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/summary: An illustration showing President Jackson dressed as a monarch with a crown holding a veto pen and trampling directly on the Constitution.
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/question: How does the cartoonist critique the President?
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/answer_1: By showing that Jackson was trying to establish a permanent royal family in the United States.
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/answer_2_correct: By suggesting his extensive use of executive power makes him a tyrant who does not respect the law.
en.lvl_3/artifact_14/answer_3: By arguing that he was too weak and cowardly to make important decisions for the country.
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/title: General Jackson Slaying the Many Headed Monster
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/log_context: A very famous political cartoon printed in 1836.
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/summary: President Jackson is shown fighting a giant snake with many heads. The evil monster represents the National Bank trying to attack the common people.
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/question: What does the giant monster in this cartoon represent?
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/answer_1: The constant threat of rebellion from angry farmers who refused to pay their taxes.
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/answer_2_correct: The corrupt National Bank and its powerful branches that Jackson desperately wanted to destroy.
en.lvl_3/artifact_15/answer_3: The growing danger of foreign armies attempting to invade the American frontier.
en.log_desc/level_2/jackson_sovereignty: Andrew Jackson said that, even after Worcester v. Georgia, states like Georgia still had the right to control their lands.
en.log_desc/level_2/jackson_enforcing: Jackson declared that it was not his role to enforce the Court's decision if it could create greater conflict.
en.log_desc/level_2/jackson_cherokee_resist: Jackson stated that, although the Cherokee used the courts, he believed moving west would protect them.
en.log_desc/level_2/jackson_indian_removal: Jackson affirmed that the Indian Removal Act was necessary to support the nation's growth and avoid future conflicts.
en.log_desc/level_3/jackson_bank_veto: Andrew Jackson declared that the national bank gave too much power to the wealthy and that he acted to protect the common people.
en.log_desc/level_3/jackson_nullification_c: Jackson stated that the Union had to be preserved and that states could not ignore federal laws.
en.log_desc/level_3/jackson_treaty_of_new_e: Jackson said that removing Native peoples to the west would prevent conflict and strengthen the nation.
en.log_desc/level_3/jackson_long_term_impac: Jackson affirmed that his decisions would expand the country and create future opportunities for growth.
